entries.title: The Love Hierarchy
entries.synopsis: A three-tier funnel governing qualification for any relationship — short or long term. Every tier must be passed in sequence. Failure at any level is disqualifying for that tier and everything above it.

Secondary factors
Tertiary factors
Sequential gates
primary secondary tertiary
each tier must be passed in sequence
boundaryConditions: The hierarchy describes a qualification sequence within each stated perspective; it is not one universal ranking shared by every person.
commonMisreadings: Passing a person's listed factors does not create attraction, consent, compatibility, or entitlement to a relationship.
pressureTests: Would the same candidate pass short-term primary factors but fail long-term secondary or tertiary factors?

entries.title: The Five Levers of SMV
entries.synopsis: Most "SMV" talk collapses a person into a single score and then argues about the decimal. The useful version is structural: your standing is built from five movable factors, then scaled by forces you mostly don't control — the clock, the market you're in, and what's actually being selected for. Raise the levers. Respect the multipliers.
phrases: Looks + Money + Status + Charm + Exposure × Clock × Market × Context
Looks Money Status Charm Exposure
clock market context
boundaryConditions: Not a real equation — a map. The "+" hides the fact that one weak factor can quietly cap the others, and the weights themselves shift with context. The arithmetic is illustrative; the structure is the point.
SMV is contextual, market-relative, and time-sensitive rather than a fixed trait.
The five levers model dating-market response, not human worth or moral worth.
commonMisreadings: A composite market estimate is not a clinical score, a universal rank, or a promise of any individual's response.
pressureTests: Does the conclusion survive a change of age band, location, platform, relationship goal, or available pool?

entries.title: Looks
entries.synopsis: The visual packet the market reads in milliseconds — and the one place a stranger’s snap judgment is, statistically, doing real work. This isn’t vanity. It’s triage: looks decide who gets considered at all, before any other factor gets a vote.
phrases: The signal that fires before you say a word.

Stop fighting the parts you can’t move and max the ones you can. Lean, groomed, well-dressed, and well-photographed beats "good bones, no effort" in the only arena that scores you: the first three seconds.
boundaryConditions: Bone structure, height, base face. Past a point, genetics set the ceiling, and pretending otherwise just sells you surgery and serums.
Looks act as a high-leverage first gate but do not by themselves supply compatibility, availability, or retention.
commonMisreadings: Looksmaxxing into paralysis. When "I’m not attractive enough" becomes the reason to never enter the market, Looks has stopped being a lever and become an alibi for staying out of the game entirely.
High looks are not equivalent to high total SMV in every market or to long-term relationship quality.
pressureTests: Is the claimed effect still present after separating initial attention from being chosen and kept?

entries.title: Face
entries.synopsis: Averageness, symmetry, and sexual dimorphism. "Average" here means mathematically composite, not forgettable — blended faces read as more attractive (Langlois & Roggman, 1990).

entries.title: Body
entries.synopsis: Composition and shape carry more signal than raw weight. The female hourglass (waist-to-hip ~0.7) and the male V-taper (shoulder-to-hip ratio) are the dimorphic cues the eye is tuned to.

entries.title: Height
entries.synopsis: A near one-directional lever for men: women’s preference for taller partners is stronger than men’s preference for shorter ones — but it’s a window, not a ladder. Very large gaps get dispreferred too.
phrases: six feet tall
under six feet
short king

entries.title: Grooming & style
entries.synopsis: The most malleable slice of Looks. Skin, hair, fit, scent, posture — the part you can move in weeks, not generations.

entries.title: Voice
entries.synopsis: An overlooked cue. Lower-pitched male voices and higher-pitched female voices read as more attractive, signaling body size and dimorphism (Puts; Feinberg).

entries.title: Age
entries.synopsis: Looks are time-stamped. This is where the Clock multiplier bites hardest — and the reason "start now" beats "start perfect."

entries.title: Money
entries.synopsis: Not the number in your account — the signal that you can provide, that your life is under control, and that the arrow points up. Money buys options and quietly raises the floor under every other factor.
phrases: Resources, stability, and the direction of both.
Fix the floor before chasing the ceiling. Stable, low-debt, and clearly-rising reads better than a leased flex on a fragile base. Then treat earning power as a multi-year build, not a weekend hack.
boundaryConditions: Where you start: family money, the local economy, your field’s ceiling. The opening hand is luck.
Money is one lever whose salience varies with life stage, market, and relationship goal.
commonMisreadings: Two failure modes, opposite directions. The wallet-as-personality flex — and the inverse cope that "she only wants money," a story that conveniently excuses building any.
Resources cannot be assumed to manufacture attraction or erase failures in every other lever.
pressureTests: Would the same result hold when income is visible but status, generosity, debt, and lifestyle fit differ?

entries.title: Income
entries.synopsis: Current earning power — the visible, askable number. Matters, but reads as less attractive than people fear when the rest is stable.

entries.title: Assets & stability
entries.synopsis: The floor: savings, low debt, no money panic. Quietly more attractive than flash, because it signals a life someone could join without rescuing.

entries.title: Trajectory
entries.synopsis: The market prices direction, not just position. "Building" and "accelerating" often beat "arrived but stalled."

entries.title: Provisioning signal
entries.synopsis: Whether a partner reads you as a stable life to join or a project to fix. This is the part Money is really standing in for.

entries.title: Spending freedom
entries.synopsis: The ability to create experiences without strain — taste, generosity, logistics. Not flexing; just not flinching.

entries.title: Status
entries.synopsis: Where you sit in the eyes of others, and the route you took to get there. Status is the most socially-read factor: you see it less in the person than in how the room reacts to them.
phrases: Your rank — and crucially, how you got it.

Chase prestige, not dominance theater. Get good at something people value, get vouched for, and let preselection talk for you. Borrowed dominance — the manufactured alpha act — reads as exactly the tell it is.
boundaryConditions: Inherited status and the prestige of where you already stand. Slow to inherit; instant to squander.
Status is audience- and context-dependent; recognition in one circle may not transfer to another.
commonMisreadings: Status-chasing that eats the self. When rank becomes the entire personality — performative dominance, status anxiety, treating people as audience — you’ve polished the signal and hollowed out the thing it was supposed to signal.
Status is not the same as virtue, intimacy, or broad public fame.
pressureTests: Does the claimed status advantage persist outside the network that recognizes it?

entries.title: Dominance
entries.synopsis: Rank through assertiveness, presence, and willingness to take space. One of two real routes to status (Henrich & Gil-White, 2001) — potent, but read warily for the long term.

entries.title: Prestige
entries.synopsis: Rank through competence and freely-given respect: being genuinely good at something people value. The other route, and the more durable one.

entries.title: Reputation
entries.synopsis: What gets said about you when you’re not in the room. Compounds slowly, forfeits fast.

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Visible evidence that others already chose you. Being wanted makes you more wanted — humans copy observed mate choices (Place et al., 2010).
phrases: taken men seem more attractive
wedding ring effect

entries.title: Leadership & network
entries.synopsis: Whether you shape rooms or just fill them, and the quality of the people who vouch for you.

entries.title: Charm
entries.synopsis: The live layer. Looks open the door; Charm decides whether you’re invited back through it. Presence, wit, warmth, calibration, and the ability to make another person actually feel something in your company.
phrases: What you do with the attention once you have it.

Get live reps. Charm does not improve in your head — it improves in real conversations where you can be misread, recover, and recalibrate. For most introverted, principled men this is the single highest-return factor, because it’s pure skill and almost nobody trains it on purpose.
boundaryConditions: Baseline temperament, social wiring, neurodivergence. Some people genuinely start with a steeper hill, and that’s worth naming honestly.
Charm can improve conversion after interaction but cannot reliably rescue a profile that never reaches interaction.
commonMisreadings: Charm weaponized into manipulation — "game" that treats people as locks to be picked. The moment technique loses warmth it reads as exactly what it is, and it stops working on anyone worth keeping.
Social skill is neither irrelevant nor an unlimited substitute for all threshold traits.
pressureTests: Did the source observe an actual interaction, or infer charm's power from profiles that never met?

entries.title: Conversation & wit
entries.synopsis: Making time spent with you better than time without you. Humor does more work here than almost anything else.

entries.title: Calibration
entries.synopsis: Reading signals and escalating at the right speed. The gap between "smooth" and "creepy" is almost entirely timing, not content.

entries.title: Emotional steadiness
entries.synopsis: Not leaking neediness under ambiguity. Calm is attractive precisely because it’s rare and hard to fake.

entries.title: Warmth
entries.synopsis: The capacity to make someone feel safe, seen, and at ease — the half of Charm the strategy crowd keeps forgetting.

entries.title: Presence
entries.synopsis: Whether people remember the feeling of being around you after you’ve left the room.

entries.title: Exposure
entries.synopsis: The factor nobody romantic wants to admit is decisive: surface area. The best profile in the world scores nothing if it’s never seen. Exposure is the denominator sitting under every other factor — and usually the most neglected.
phrases: How many qualified people actually encounter you.

Increase qualified surface area and then act on it. Better photos, the right channels, recurring social environments, consistent initiative. For most people who feel stuck, the bottleneck isn’t their score — it’s that almost no one is seeing it.
boundaryConditions: The market you’re physically in right now — its size, age pool, and ratio. Real constraints, not excuses, but constraints.
Exposure multiplies opportunities to be evaluated; it does not guarantee favorable evaluation.
commonMisreadings: Spray-and-pray volume with zero standards — or its mirror image: treating low exposure as proof the market is rigged, rather than the one variable most under your own control.
A lack of outcomes under very low exposure is not clean evidence of low desirability.
pressureTests: How many relevant people could actually encounter and evaluate the person under study?

entries.title: Geography & sex ratio
entries.synopsis: The local supply and demand you’re embedded in. Your value is relative to the ratio around you (Guttentag & Secord, 1983).

entries.title: Volume of contact
entries.synopsis: How many plausible, available people you actually cross paths with — qualified encounters, not raw foot traffic.

entries.title: The online funnel
entries.synopsis: Apps as a high-volume, brutally-sorted channel: effective, and merciless about the desirability hierarchy.
phrases: matches on the apps
likes on Hinge
swipe right

entries.title: Recurring environments
entries.synopsis: Repeated contact beats one-off events. Propinquity and mere exposure quietly manufacture attraction over time.

entries.title: Initiative
entries.synopsis: The multiplier on everything above. Surface area you never act on is just scenery.

entries.title: The Clock
entries.synopsis: Every factor is time-stamped. Looks and fertility cues are front-loaded; money, status, and prestige accrue with age. Your score isn't a fixed point — it's a trajectory, and the slope can matter as much as the height.
phrases: SMV is a curve, not a constant.
boundaryConditions: Use it to respect timing, not to panic. The clock rewards starting now over starting "when you're finally ready."
Age effects vary by sex, goal, fertility plans, cohort, and market; they are slopes and trade-offs, not one cliff.
pressureTests: Is age being used as a population trend, an individual destiny, or a proxy for an unstated goal?

entries.title: The Market
entries.synopsis: There is no absolute SMV. The same profile is a 6 in one city and an 8 in another, depending on the sex ratio, the age pool, and the competition around it. The market sets the exchange rate; you just hold the currency.
phrases: Your score is always relative.
boundaryConditions: A brutal local market is data, not a verdict. Sometimes the highest-return move isn't raising your score — it's changing the market you're scored in.
The same profile can face different scarcity, competition, and norms in different markets.
pressureTests: Would the claim reverse in a market with a different sex ratio, geography, app mix, or relationship norm?

entries.title: The Context
entries.synopsis: The five factors aren't weighted the same in every situation. For short-term attraction, Looks, dominance, and immediacy spike. For long-term, stability, prestige, warmth, and reliability take over. A profile tuned for one can underperform in the other.
phrases: The weights themselves change.
boundaryConditions: Know which game you're playing. Optimizing your whole self for short-term metrics, then wondering why long-term keeps failing, is a category error.
Traits are weighted differently in stranger markets, social circles, apps, hookups, and long-term selection.
pressureTests: Which stage and venue produced the observed response, and is the source generalizing beyond it?

entries.title: The Conversion Ladder
entries.synopsis: A stage model for separating attention, desire, choice, and durability — the lens the rest of this page sits inside. It is not a universal love equation; it is a debugging tool. A person can win one rung and fail the next, which is why app attention, sexual interest, commitment, and relationship stability should never be treated as the same signal.
phrases: attention is not desire
desire is not commitment
choice is not retention
stuck in the friend zone
friendzoned
boundaryConditions: The ladder distinguishes stages analytically; real relationships can loop, stall, regress, or skip observable steps.
commonMisreadings: Being seen or receiving messages is not proof of desire, selection, compatibility, or durable commitment.
pressureTests: At exactly which transition did the evidence occur, and what evidence shows movement to the next stage?

entries.title: The Interaction Gate
entries.synopsis: Profiles, checklists, and calculators can reject a known mismatch. In the available speed-dating evidence, pre-date traits and preferences did not reliably rank pair-specific desire. The operating distinction is simple: pre-contact evidence may screen out; richer interaction must select in.
boundaryConditions: Profiles and calculators can reject known mismatches, but positive compatibility remains indeterminate until live interaction.
commonMisreadings: A high profile score or checklist match cannot establish chemistry, felt safety, or mutual ease.

sourceLinks.label: Joel, Eastwick & Finkel (2017), Psychological Science
Baxter et al. (2022), PNAS

pressureTests: What changed after voice, timing, mannerisms, conflict style, and reciprocal interest became observable?

entries.title: The Readiness Gate
entries.synopsis: A good candidate and an available candidate are not the same state. For a commitment goal, pair-specific interest must clear one gate and present willingness and capacity to build must clear another. Chemistry without readiness is not a delayed yes or a renovation project.
boundaryConditions: A viable match can still fail when one or both people lack availability, intention, capacity, or timing.
commonMisreadings: Readiness failure does not prove either person is defective, nor does potential override a present no.

sourceLinks.label: Hadden, Agnew & Tan (2018), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

pressureTests: If attraction and compatibility are held constant, is there evidence of present capacity and reciprocal intent?

entries.title: The 7–7 Rule
entries.synopsis: A binary qualification gate for serious long-term candidates: physical attractiveness ≥ 7 and the personality composite ≥ 7. The two sides are scored independently — a high score on one never compensates for a low score on the other. The personality side is an aggregate, not a single trait, so one charming quality can’t carry a weak overall composite.
boundaryConditions: The thresholds are a practical LE heuristic, not a population law or guarantee of a successful relationship.
commonMisreadings: Two sufficient scores do not bypass consent, timing, attraction asymmetry, or the Interaction Gate.
pressureTests: Can a candidate clear both model thresholds yet fail because the measured dimensions omit a decisive live factor?

entries.title: Sub-5 Auto Disqualification
entries.synopsis: A score below 5 in any single important component — a load-bearing sub-factor of the looks or personality composite — signals active incompatibility, not just weakness. It catches what an average launders: a 7 composite can be hiding a 3 underneath. It doesn’t matter how strong everything else is — one important component under 5 trips the floor.
boundaryConditions: The rule represents hard personal minimums inside LE's scoring model, not a moral judgment or a universal cutoff.
commonMisreadings: A below-threshold model result does not make a person lesser or predict every evaluator's decision.
pressureTests: Is the disqualifying dimension truly non-negotiable for this evaluator, or an averaged preference treated as absolute?

entries.title: Treatment Markup System
entries.synopsis: A dual-use model. First it scores: each person’s base is looks + treatment, and whoever brings the stronger treatment earns a markup on top — behavior is a real value-add, not décor. Then it pairs: read Person A and Person B as a couple and ask whether they actually match.
boundaryConditions: Differential effort can reveal perceived leverage, but context, personality, resources, safety, and strategy can also affect treatment.
commonMisreadings: Money spent, pursuit intensity, or politeness alone is not a clean meter of attraction.
pressureTests: Does the treatment difference persist across comparable contexts and costs, or is one anecdote carrying the inference?

entries.title: Looks Rating Evaluation System
entries.synopsis: A looks score is not static, but it is not infinitely fluid either. Every rating carries a support floor and a resistance ceiling that bound how perception drifts over time. Initial evaluations are highly accurate — but bias, familiarity, and behavior all apply pressure within the band.
boundaryConditions: The scale is an anchor for disciplined comparison, not an objective biometric truth or universal verdict.
commonMisreadings: A numeric looks estimate should not be presented as more precise than the inputs or evaluator agreement allow.
pressureTests: How much does the rating move across evaluators, styling, photos, age, and in-person presentation?

entries.title: The Parity Rule
entries.synopsis: The 7–7 tells you what a top long-term partner has to clear; it doesn’t tell you who you get. The Parity Rule does: your realistic ideal is your own coordinates. A 6–6 (looks-6, personality-6) pairs with a 6–6, a 4–4 with a 4–4, down the ladder to 1–1. The 7–7 is the universal aspiration; parity is the attainable one. You don’t marry the gate — you marry your tier.
boundaryConditions: Assortative matching is a distributional tendency with exceptions, trade-offs, and measurement error.
commonMisreadings: Population clustering near parity does not decree who any individual may attract or retain.
pressureTests: What compensating lever, selection channel, or measurement error explains stable off-parity couples?

entries.title: The Spiderman Effect
entries.synopsis: The Parity Rule says you can’t objectively attain a 7–7 as a 6–6. The Spiderman Effect says you can attain one subjectively: to another 6–6 you read as their 7–7, and they read as yours. Two equals, each pointing at the other as the special one — the meme made literal. As long as both believe it, it functions as real, because attraction runs partly on perception, not only on the consensus score.
boundaryConditions: Repeated exposure and social context can change evaluation only when real contact occurs; proximity is not entitlement.
commonMisreadings: Familiarity does not guarantee attraction and must not be used to excuse persistence after rejection.
pressureTests: Would the outcome survive without repeated low-pressure contact, community trust, or constrained alternatives?

entries.title: SMV Matching
entries.synopsis: How attractiveness sorts the market. Score looks as a within-sex percentile — a 7 is the 70th percentile of one’s own sex, not an absolute. Across already-paired couples, partners’ rated looks correlate at r ≈ 0.4 — moderate, real matching.
phrases: out of your league
out of his league
settle for less
boundaryConditions: The five layers organize recurring patterns; they do not collapse into one deterministic equation for every pair.
commonMisreadings: Market leverage, attention, and partner quality are distinct outcomes and cannot be substituted for one another.
pressureTests: Which layer actually explains the case, and what observed exception would the layer fail to explain?

entries.title: The Matching Curve
entries.synopsis: Within-sex looks matching among already-paired couples. One curve — it applies identically to men and women.

entries.title: The Attention Market
entries.synopsis: Who gets noticed before anyone pairs. Attention is not the same thing as commitment.
boundaryConditions: Online attention distributions depend on platform mechanics and do not directly measure desire, selection, or offline pairing.
commonMisreadings: Message or swipe concentration is not proof that the same minority monopolizes relationships.
pressureTests: Does the pattern persist in actual dates and relationships after platform sorting and inactive accounts are removed?

entries.title: The Option Pool
entries.synopsis: Who can be converted from attention into realistic dates or commitment. Options and pairings are different things.
boundaryConditions: Visible options are not equivalent to viable, reciprocal, available, or compatible options.
commonMisreadings: A large inbox or local population should not be counted as a large pool of relationship candidates.
pressureTests: After reciprocity, goal, location, attraction, readiness, and compatibility filters, how many options remain?

entries.title: The Charm Ceiling
entries.synopsis: How far can game / charm actually carry you, and where does it cap? Part 1 takes a Blackpill creator’s looks-vs-game model at face value; Part 2 draws the research model on its own axes. The source is strictly male-perspective (the man judged, women as acceptors), so Part 1 follows that; Part 2 is tabbable to either the male or female view.
phrases: Right about the stranger-market arena it maps — apps, cold approach — but false generalized to all of dating. Charm is access-gated, not value-gated.
boundaryConditions: Charm matters most after interaction and has limits when a hard attraction or safety threshold is not met.
commonMisreadings: The ceiling does not mean personality is irrelevant; it distinguishes access to interaction from conversion within it.
pressureTests: Is charm being credited for creating access, or for improving outcomes among people who already had access?

entries.title: The Status Trade
entries.synopsis: Beyond looks and charm, overall mate value is a blend — and this is where the framework’s opening promise pays off: the “trading up” people notice enters through status. We take the canonical Red Pill hypergamy claim, then check it.
phrases: A real status tilt treated as an innate, immutable iron law. Women do weight status more — but educational hypergamy has reversed and the provider norm is halving, so it is fading, not hardening.
boundaryConditions: Cross-lever compensation is partial and context-specific; no lever universally purchases another person's desire.
commonMisreadings: A statistical pairing trade-off is not a transactional entitlement.
pressureTests: Does the apparent trade remain after age, network, shared goals, and direct attraction are considered?

entries.title: The Men’s Strike
entries.synopsis: The hypothetical that haunts the manosphere: if men acted in coordination and simply stopped — stopped approaching, asking, initiating — the market would seize, women would feel the absence, and the terms would reset in men’s favor. It is a real question with a measurable spine, because initiation is overwhelmingly male — so withdrawal is, in principle, men’s to attempt.

entries.title: The Abundance Trap
entries.synopsis: The apps’ founding promise was that more options would make finding a partner easier. The trap is that visible abundance changes the chooser: with the whole distribution on screen, evaluation replaces connection, the next profile taxes the current one, and standards drift upward without the underlying market moving at all. Both sexes run this loop — whoever holds the fatter option stack runs it harder.
