entries.title: Does "like me for me" run both ways?
entries.synopsis: The double standard is real; the one-way framing isn't. In Li et al.'s (2002) budget studies nobody buys 'as-is' acceptance: with tight budgets women spend first on status and resources, men on physical attractiveness; kindness and intelligence are necessities for both — necessary, not sufficient, the kind-but-awkward man's exact problem.
phrases: "I want someone who likes me for me" usually means: accept all my flaws — but that grace rarely runs the other direction. The same person still wants you socially smooth, confident, funny on demand, and good at flirting, even if you're naturally awkward.

"I just want a man who likes me for me" is fair — but notice whether the grace runs both ways. Often it means: accept all my flaws, while I still expect you to be tall, fit, confident, funny, successful, and smooth.
boundaryConditions: Li's budgets tested kindness and intelligence, not social skills or charisma, so the 'awkwardness disqualifies even the kind guy' clause is inferred from necessity-not-sufficiency logic rather than directly tested.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: "I want someone who likes me for me" usually means: accept all my flaws — but that grace rarely runs the other direction. The same person still wants you socially smooth, confident, funny on demand, and good at flirting, even if you're naturally awkward.

sourceLinks.label: Li, Bailey, Kenrick & Linsenmeier (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — budget paradigm: physical attractiveness a necessity for men, status/resources for women, kindness and intelligence necessities for both sexes
Eastwick, Luchies, Finkel & Hunt (2014), Psychological Bulletin — meta-analysis (k=97): attractiveness predicts romantic evaluations at r≈.40 for both sexes; sex differences tiny and nonsignificant

entries.title: Does a flood of attention inflate self-assessed value?
entries.synopsis: The mechanism is real. In controlled experiments (Kavanagh, Robins & Ellis, 2010), being accepted by attractive opposite-sex others raised participants' mating aspirations, mediated by a lift in state self-esteem — so incoming attention genuinely inflates self-assessed value and pushes standards up. In real markets both sexes already message partners about 25% more desirable than themselves (Bruch & Newman, 2018).
phrases: When average women have tons of options, constant attention, and a crowd of guys orbiting them, it inflates their sense of their own value — even when they're not particularly special.
When your inbox is full and there's always another option, it's easy to conclude you're more in-demand than you actually are — and to keep raising the bar accordingly.
boundaryConditions: Kavanagh et al. is a single two-experiment paper — the mechanism is established but caps at 'evidence,' and the 'average women'/simp-economy causal story is framing, not tested. A women-specific mate-value-feedback study (Pers. Individ. Differ.) that would corroborate directly was paywalled this session (403), so it is uncited.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: When average women have tons of options, constant attention, and a crowd of guys orbiting them, it inflates their sense of their own value — even when they're not particularly special. The male thirst is the supply that props up the leverage, and that power dynamic goes to a lot of their heads.

sourceLinks.label: Kavanagh, Robins & Ellis (2010), J. Personality & Social Psychology — experimental acceptance by attractive opposite-sex confederates raised mating aspirations, mediated by state self-esteem
Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances — both sexes pursue partners ~25% more desirable than themselves

entries.title: Is "the bar is in hell" low standards — or selective ones?
entries.synopsis: Attraction really does bend the ruler. Meta-analytically, physically attractive people are judged and treated more positively across domains (Langlois et al., 2000), and attractiveness predicts live romantic desire at r≈.40 for both sexes (Eastwick et al., 2014) — so tolerance is conditioned on attraction, not uniformly low. 'Selective, not low' is the correct reframe.
phrases: It doesn't hold up: if the bar were really that low, they'd date anyone. What it actually means is the bar is in hell for guys they're not attracted to — and on the roof for the ones they are.
If your bar were genuinely low, you'd date almost anyone; you don't. What's actually happening is that the bar sits on the floor for men you're not attracted to and on the roof for the ones you are.
boundaryConditions: The halo is robust and cross-cultural but modest in size, and it is universal — not specific to women judging men, which weakens the gendered framing. Mazzella & Feingold's (1994) meta-analysis (attractive defendants punished less leniently, d≈.12) would directly support the 'forgive transgressions' point but its journal page was paywalled this session…
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: It doesn't hold up: if the bar were really that low, they'd date anyone. What it actually means is the bar is in hell for guys they're not attracted to — and on the roof for the ones they are. They'll overlook massive red flags for a hot or charismatic guy, then turn around and say a normal, decent guy doesn't meet their standards.

sourceLinks.label: Langlois, Kalakanis, Rubenstein, Larson, Hallam & Smoot (2000), Psychological Bulletin — meta-analysis: attractive people are judged and treated more positively, with cross-cultural rater agreement
Eastwick, Luchies, Finkel & Hunt (2014), Psychological Bulletin — attractiveness predicts romantic evaluation at r≈.40, near-identical across sexes

entries.title: Does her abundance hide how hard the market is for average men?
entries.synopsis: The asymmetry is real. In a Tinder field experiment women accumulated matches rapidly while men accrued them slowly (Tyson et al., 2016); in a full dating market men overwhelmingly message up, where replies from more-desirable women never top 21% and men hear back twice as often from less-desirable ones (Bruch & Newman, 2018). So women do receive more attention and average men face steep odds.
phrases: Most women genuinely don't grasp how rough the dating market has gotten for average men — because their own experience is the opposite. When you personally have endless options, you assume everyone does: "I get tons of attention, so men must too."

If you get steady attention, it's natural to assume men have it just as easy — so when you hear that a huge share of average guys get almost nothing, it sounds exaggerated. It isn't. The market is brutally lopsided, and your abundance is the exact thing that hides that from you.
boundaryConditions: Objective asymmetry is well-supported (apps especially); the perception/'abundance blinds them' half is an untested inference. Tyson's often-quoted exact match rates (~0.6% men vs ~10.5% women) sit in the paper body, not the abstract I could load, so the ruling leans on the abstract's directional finding plus Bruch & Newman's verified reply-rate numbers.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Most women genuinely don't grasp how rough the dating market has gotten for average men — because their own experience is the opposite. When you personally have endless options, you assume everyone does: "I get tons of attention, so men must too."

oversimplified: If you get steady attention, it's natural to assume men have it just as easy — so when you hear that a huge share of average guys get almost nothing, it sounds exaggerated. It isn't. The market is brutally lopsided, and your abundance is the exact thing that hides that from you.

sourceLinks.label: Tyson, Perta, Haddadi & Seto (2016), ASONAM/arXiv — Tinder curated-profile experiment: women accumulate matches rapidly, men slowly
Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances — men overwhelmingly message more-desirable women; reply rate up-hierarchy never exceeds 21%

entries.title: Does a man's dating window narrow — and does sitting out compound?
entries.synopsis: Partly grounded, partly not. Women do prefer slightly older partners within a narrower age band (Antfolk, 2017), and romantically/sexually inexperienced adults are stigmatized and less desired (Gesselman et al., 2017) — so 'they screen for an established, experienced man' holds.
phrases: Younger guys still in their early 20s have years to course-correct; by your early-to-mid 30s that luxury is mostly gone — the window has narrowed. Most women looking to settle down are aiming at men roughly 28–38, but they specifically want men who already have their act…
boundaryConditions: Antfolk supports slightly-older, narrow-range female preferences but gives no specific 28–38 band; Bruch & Newman's age-desirability curve (male desirability rising with age) actively cuts against the 'narrowing window,' though it measures online-message desirability rather than settle-down marriageability.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Younger guys still in their early 20s have years to course-correct; by your early-to-mid 30s that luxury is mostly gone — the window has narrowed. Most women looking to settle down are aiming at men roughly 28–38, but they specifically want men who already have their act together: career, social skills, dating experience.

sourceLinks.label: Antfolk (2017), Evolutionary Psychology — women prefer slightly older partners in a narrower band; men prefer women in their 20s and widen with age
Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances — male desirability rises with age, peaking near 50 (counter-evidence to a narrowing 30s window)
Gesselman, Webster & Garcia (2017), Journal of Sex Research — sexually/romantically inexperienced adults are stigmatized and less desired as partners

entries.title: Is dating-market entitlement a women-only problem?
entries.synopsis: Behavioral data back the symmetry. Analyzing four U.S. cities, Bruch & Newman (2018) found men and women message partners 26% and 23% more desirable than themselves — near-identical aiming-up. Kreager et al. (2014) likewise found both sexes pursue the most desirable partners regardless of their own standing, and Epley & Whitchurch (2008) showed people literally recognize a beautified version of their own face as real.
phrases: Yes, a lot of women carry inflated standards — the "6 feet, six figures" checklist while bringing little to the table themselves. But entitlement isn't a women-only problem.
boundaryConditions: Bruch/Newman and Kreager are large behavioral-trace datasets from single dating sites, not representative population surveys, and the 26/23% figures reflect messaging behavior rather than stated entitlement; self-enhancement magnitude (Epley) varies by measure.

sourceLinks.label: Bruch & Newman (2018), Science Advances — both sexes message partners ~25% more desirable than themselves (men 26%, women 23%).

Kreager, Cavanagh, Yen & Yu (2014), Journal of Marriage and Family — both sexes send messages to the most socially desirable partners regardless of their own desirability; women initiate 4x less than men.
Epley & Whitchurch (2008), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin — people recognize an attractively enhanced version of their own face as their true face (self-enhancement).

entries.title: Do men and women avoid commitment for the same reason?
entries.synopsis: The sex-typed split is half-real. Schmitt's 48-nation study (N=14,059) confirms men score reliably higher on unrestricted sociosexuality — the 'variety' motive is well-founded and cross-culturally robust. Apostolou et al. (2020) likewise found men more often single to 'flirt around' or avoid family life.
phrases: A lot of women stay uncommitted because they're holding out for a better option: they'll keep a decent "good enough" guy around as a backup while they keep looking, never fully locking in because they're always wondering if someone higher-value is a swipe away.
boundaryConditions: Schmitt's sociosexuality sex difference is robust and cross-cultural, but the specific 'women optimize/keep a backup vs men seek variety' dichotomy rests on single studies (Apostolou; Dibble) that partly conflict — back-burner counts run opposite to the claim's gendering. Regrade risk if stronger reasons-for-single sex-difference data emerges.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A lot of women stay uncommitted because they're holding out for a better option: they'll keep a decent "good enough" guy around as a backup while they keep looking, never fully locking in because they're always wondering if someone higher-value is a swipe away.

sourceLinks.label: Schmitt (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences — 48 nations, N=14,059; men's higher unrestricted sociosexuality is large and cross-culturally universal.
Apostolou, O & Esposito (2020), Frontiers in Psychology — N=648 singles; men more often single to 'flirt around'/avoid family life, women more often 'too picky'/fearing hurt.
Dibble & Drouin (2014), Computers in Human Behavior — N=374; men reported more 'back burners' (alternative partners kept in reserve) than women.

entries.title: How much is a woman's explicit first move worth?
entries.synopsis: Rarity and weight check out; the 'men ignore it' half is shakier. Kreager et al. (2014) found women send first messages four times less often than men — and those who do initiate connect with more desirable partners, so an explicit move is both rare and a costly, informative signal.
phrases: A woman making the first explicit move — not a covert signal, but actually saying it — is genuinely rare, so when it happens it tends to carry more weight than men give it.
boundaryConditions: Kreager's 4x initiation gap is one large study; female-initiation rarity is widely observed but only this source was verified here. Haselton & Buss concerns overperception of ambiguous cues, not dismissal of explicit stated moves, so the tension with 'men wave it off' is suggestive rather than decisive.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: A woman making the first explicit move — not a covert signal, but actually saying it — is genuinely rare, so when it happens it tends to carry more weight than men give it. When a woman compliments your looks unprompted, asks for your number, or says something like "you smell nice," she's usually spent real social risk to do it.

sourceLinks.label: Kreager, Cavanagh, Yen & Yu (2014), Journal of Marriage and Family — women send first messages 4x less often than men; women who initiate connect with more desirable partners.
Haselton & Buss (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology — men overperceive women's sexual intent; women underperceive men's commitment (error management theory).

entries.title: Should men wait for a choosing signal before approaching?
entries.synopsis: Choosing signals are useful evidence, not an admission ticket. Moore’s field observations found that women who signaled more were approached more often, so repeated, person-specific cues raise the odds that an opening is welcome. But Hall’s two studies found actual flirting harder to identify than nonflirting; making a detectable green light mandatory would turn ordinary uncertainty into paralysis.
phrases: Men should wait for a woman to give a choosing signal before approaching. Women commonly initiate indirectly, and approaching without that green light mostly creates low-yield or unwanted attention.
boundaryConditions: No direct head-to-head outcome study comparing a strict signal-required strategy with a respectful once-and-done approach was found, which prevents a hard-data grade and makes a synthetic truth percentage inappropriate.
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: Men should wait for a woman to give a choosing signal before approaching. Women commonly initiate indirectly, and approaching without that green light mostly creates low-yield or unwanted attention.

sourceLinks.label: Moore (1985), Ethology and Sociobiology — field observations: women who displayed solicitation signals more often were approached more often across four social contexts
Hall, Xing & Brooks (2014), Communication Research — two studies found actual flirting harder to identify than nonflirting for participants and outside observers
Sinclair & Frieze (2005), Sex Roles — 241 pursuer/target accounts: pursuers over-reported reciprocation and under-reported rejection as courtship became unwanted persistence

entries.title: Do women regret casual sex while men regret passing it up?
entries.synopsis: The mirror pattern is robust, not destiny. Galperin et al.’s three studies (Ns = 200, 395, and 24,230) found more casual-sex action regret among women and more missed-opportunity regret among men; the Norwegian replication and later two-wave study reproduced the average sex-linked pattern. “Tendency” is essential: it does not predict any individual, and it does not mean women usually regret casual sex.
phrases: Women have a tendency to regret casual sex they had more than men do.
Men have a tendency to regret casual sex they passed up more than women do.
boundaryConditions: Hard-data grades the replicated descriptive direction, not a proven evolutionary mechanism. Galperin’s three studies and the Norwegian replication rely on retrospective self-report; the authors’ sexual-strategies interpretation is one proposed distal explanation, not an experimental result.

sourceLinks.label: Galperin et al. (2013), Archives of Sexual Behavior — three descriptive studies (Ns = 200, 395, 24,230) found the casual-sex action/inaction regret pattern across methods and a diverse online sample
Kennair, Bendixen & Buss (2016), Evolutionary Psychology — Norwegian replication (N = 263) plus tests of gratification, worry, reputation, and sociosexuality as competing proximate correlates
Kennair, Grøntvedt & Bendixen (2021), Evolutionary Psychology — two-wave longitudinal test found no clear evidence that regret produced the predicted later mating-behavior shifts

Sagioglou & Dick (2026), Archives of Sexual Behavior — international cross-sectional study (N = 1,044): most one-night stands neutral-to-positive; heterosexual regret gap mediated chiefly by satisfaction and orgasm

entries.title: Do romance scammers mostly prey on lonely older women?
entries.synopsis: The stereotype survives on exactly one axis: check size. FTC median losses climb steeply with age — $750 per report at 18–29 up to $9,000 at 70 and over — so when older adults are taken, they are taken hardest. Targeting cuts the other way: 52% of online daters say they’ve come across a suspected scammer, and men under 50 top the table at 63%, against 44% of women of any age.
phrases: The romance-scam victim is the lonely grandma wiring her savings to a fake soldier overseas. Young men grew up online — they can smell a catfish a mile away, and scammers don’t waste time on them.
boundaryConditions: Axes kept honest: Pew measures self-reported encounters with SUSPECTED scammers (perception, not completed victimization); the FTC counts voluntary reports, and only ~4.8% of mass-market fraud victims complain to any authority (Anderson 2021, cited in both spotlights), so age differences in reporting propensity shade every count — the report mix by age is…
commonMisreadings: oversimplified: The romance-scam victim is the lonely grandma wiring her savings to a fake soldier overseas. Young men grew up online — they can smell a catfish a mile away, and scammers don’t waste time on them.

sourceLinks.label: Pew Research Center (Feb 2023), “Key findings about online dating in the U.S.” — 52% of users encountered a suspected scammer; men under 50 highest at 63% (men 50+: 47%; women of any age: 44%); n = 6,034
FTC Data Spotlight (Feb 2022) — 2021 romance scams: record $547M reported; median individual loss by age from $750 (18–29) to $9,000 (70+); 18–29 reports up more than tenfold since 2017
FTC Data Spotlight (Feb 2023) — 2022: nearly 70,000 reports, $1.3B reported losses, median $4,400; sextortion reports over six times as likely from 18–29 as from 30+, population-normalized

entries.title: The Black Pill
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill is constraint awareness pushed toward terminal certainty. It notices that looks, early impressions, social sorting, and fixed traits matter more than polite society admits. Its useful part is realism about hard floors. Its failure is turning disadvantage into destiny.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: use Black Pill insight to identify real constraints, then return to the remaining agency. Do not confuse clear sight with a death sentence.
LE preserves constraint awareness while rejecting terminal certainty, moral ranking, and the claim that every outcome is fixed.
commonMisreadings: Total fatalism: A model that makes you less alive, less warm, and less capable has started eating the person using it.
A lens that identifies hard constraints is not itself proof that effort, context, exposure, or probability no longer matter.
pressureTests: What observable outcome would falsify the terminal version of the claim without denying the underlying constraint?

entries.title: The Height Pill
entries.synopsis: Height is the Black Pill’s favorite exhibit, and not by accident: it is a real, measurable advantage you genuinely cannot change. Women pull toward taller men more than men pull toward shorter women, and the male-taller norm shows up in almost every couple — far beyond what chance alone would produce. The lens is right that it matters and right that it’s fixed.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: count height honestly as a fixed input you can’t move — then stop relitigating it and spend the effort on the four factors you can. See the height-preference data and the Looks factor.
commonMisreadings: “It’s over under six feet” is fatalism: The premium is a window, not a ladder. The height–success curve is curvilinear: the very shortest men are penalized, but the optimum is only moderately above average — and extremely tall men get screened out too, by shorter women.

entries.title: The Face Pill
entries.synopsis: The Black Pill’s deepest fixation is the face — and its core mistake is treating it as one thing: bone. But a face is a stack of layers. The skull is the bottom one; on top sit skin and soft tissue, then framing and grooming, then the harmony of the whole — plus a side profile a front photo never shows. Raters integrate the stack, not the cephalogram.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: count the bone honestly as the one fixed layer — then stop relitigating it and work the three that move. And remember even the bone mostly prices the first glance. See The Bone Pill, checked and the Looks factor.
commonMisreadings: “Your bone-score is your fate”: The looksmaxxing pill collapses all four layers into the skull, freezes it, and scores it to a PSL decimal that “ends” you. Three of the four layers are improvable, single bones explain little alone, and the shared score itself dissolves once someone actually knows you. A real input is laundered into a sealed verdict.

entries.title: Just Be First
entries.synopsis: A timing exploit that can override normal SMV matching. The person who arrives before comparison pressure and full market calibration can form a bond that the open market might never have produced.
boundaryConditions: Important: this is not a moral ideal or a seduction recommendation. It is a structural story about timing, calibration, and why some mismatches survive because they formed before the open market could price them.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: The Red Pill treats dating as a market shaped by incentives, asymmetry, self-presentation, leverage, and strategic behavior. Its useful part is agency: improve the offer, read signals, understand incentives. Its failure mode is contempt dressed up as realism.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: use Red Pill insight to become more effective, not less humane. If it makes you sharper but colder, you are losing part of the game.
Descriptive patterns and strategies remain probabilistic and cannot override autonomy, consent, safety, or individual variation.
commonMisreadings: Contempt as doctrine: Strategy becomes poison when it loses empathy and starts treating people as enemies instead of people with incentives.
A strategy that improves odds does not create entitlement to another person's response.
pressureTests: Would the strategy still be defensible if the other person's agency and full information were made explicit?

entries.title: Hypergamy
entries.synopsis: The tendency to seek upward in status, resources, desirability, or perceived mate value. Useful as a pressure concept; dangerous when treated as a cartoon law.

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Interest can rise when other people visibly want you. Social proof does not create all attraction, but it can change how value is read.

entries.title: Frame
entries.synopsis: The ability to hold your center without begging the room to validate you. At its best, calm self-command; at its worst, performative dominance.

entries.title: The Blue Pill
entries.synopsis: The Blue Pill treats romance as sincere, fair, moral, and personality-driven. Its useful part is warmth: love is not just sorting math, and people need trust, affection, kindness, and safety. Its failure is denying the thresholds that decide who gets considered in the first place.
boundaryConditions: Operating rule: keep the heart. Drop the denial. The synthesis needs romance, but it also needs eyes.
Hope, character, and compatibility can matter without erasing attraction thresholds, market structure, or timing.
commonMisreadings: Fair-world comfort: Kindness is not a substitute for attraction. Personality matters, but usually after a first filter has been passed.
Rejecting fatalism does not require pretending that every preference is negotiable or that effort guarantees selection.
pressureTests: What observed rejection or selection pattern would the optimistic account need to explain rather than dismiss?

entries.title: Just be yourself
entries.synopsis: Healthy when it means authenticity. Harmful when it means refusing to improve presentation, social skill, standards, or exposure.

entries.title: Personality matters
entries.synopsis: True but incomplete. Personality can deepen, convert, and sustain attraction. It does not always create initial consideration from nothing.

entries.title: The right person
entries.synopsis: Useful as patience, dangerous as passivity. The right person still has to meet you, notice you, want you, and choose you.

entries.title: SMV (Sexual Market Value)
entries.synopsis: Your desirability as priced by the dating market — looks, money, status, charm, exposure, scaled by timing and competition. A market read, not a measure of human worth.

entries.title: Assortative mating
entries.synopsis: The tendency to pair with someone of similar overall value. On looks alone the average couple matches (r ≈ 0.4) rather than one side relentlessly trading up.

entries.title: The Wall
entries.synopsis: The claim that a woman’s value falls off a cliff around 30. Real as a slope, false as a cliff — and it measures stranger-attention, not whether she actually pairs.

entries.title: Conversion Ladder
entries.synopsis: The stage model separating being seen, noticed, desired, chosen, and kept. It keeps attention, attraction, commitment, and retention from being confused.

entries.title: The Interaction Gate
entries.synopsis: Use profiles and scores to screen out known incompatibility; use richer interaction to learn pair-specific chemistry, ease, and reciprocity. A hard boundary stays hard, and nobody is owed a meeting.

entries.title: The Readiness Gate
entries.synopsis: For a commitment goal, interest and present willingness to build are separate gates. “Not ready” is a current boundary, not a delayed yes or a renovation project.

entries.title: The Good-News Rule
entries.synopsis: Celebrate before you evaluate: notice a partner’s win, recognize why it matters, ask a genuine follow-up, then celebrate in a form they can receive. Practical caution can follow without swallowing the moment.

entries.title: Attention
entries.synopsis: Market signal before selection: views, likes, messages, glances, replies. Attention can be abundant and still low-intent; scarce and still high-quality.

entries.title: Desire
entries.synopsis: The felt pull toward someone. It is warmer and narrower than attention, but still not the same thing as commitment or long-term fit.

entries.title: Commitment
entries.synopsis: Selection over alternatives. Someone can desire you without choosing you; commitment is where attraction starts paying opportunity cost.

entries.title: Pairing
entries.synopsis: The outcome where two people actually form a couple. Pairing data answers a different question than app attention, casual access, or fantasy preference.

entries.title: Stranger market
entries.synopsis: The arena where people judge with little or no exposure: apps, cold approach, first glance. It prices looks and status hardest because almost nothing else has time to compound.

entries.title: Social-circle market
entries.synopsis: The arena where repeated exposure lets charm, trust, competence, and familiarity modify the first read. Slower, less scalable, and often more forgiving than the stranger market.

entries.title: Sex recession
entries.synopsis: The rise in young adults reporting no sex in the past year, especially visible among young men. It is the attention deficit made measurable, not proof that everyone is doomed.

entries.title: Cope
entries.synopsis: Any comforting story used to dodge a hard truth. A useful scalpel — but “that’s cope” is itself often used to wave away evidence that complicates the blackpill.

entries.title: The 7–7 Rule
entries.synopsis: The long-term qualification gate: looks ≥ 7 and personality composite ≥ 7, scored independently — a high score on one never buys back the other. A rule about frequency, not a law.

entries.title: Sub-5 (Auto Disqualification)
entries.synopsis: One important component under 5 trips the floor no matter how strong the rest is — averages launder weak points. Binds only if you clear 5 yourself; below that, Parity overrides it.

entries.title: The Parity Rule
entries.synopsis: Your realistic ideal is your own coordinates: a 6–6 pairs with a 6–6. The 7–7 is the universal aspiration; parity is the attainable one. You don’t marry the gate — you marry your tier.

entries.title: The Spiderman Effect
entries.synopsis: To another 6–6 you read as their 7–7, and they as yours. Mutual belief makes the subjective upgrade function as real — the humane resolution of parity’s cap.

entries.title: Treatment Markup
entries.synopsis: How you treat a partner earns a real markup on top of base value — enough to clear a parity bracket, never enough to turn a 4 into an 8. Behavior is value-add, not décor.

entries.title: The Sham
entries.synopsis: A relationship that persists without the thing it appears to be about — motive holding it up (hard sham) or a mismatch nobody names (soft sham). Not a bad relationship: one the attraction model can’t account for.

entries.title: Clock, Market, Context
entries.synopsis: The three multipliers that scale all five levers: your timing, the market you’re standing in, and what that market selects for. Raise the levers; respect the multipliers.

entries.title: The Great Unbundling
entries.synopsis: The historical arc: marriage once bundled sex, children, economics, and adult standing into one contract — and the last two centuries pulled the functions loose one by one.

entries.title: Third places
entries.synopsis: The venues that weren’t home or work — church, club, league, corner bar — where couples used to form for free. They emptied out before the apps won; the apps won partly by default.

entries.title: Situationship
entries.synopsis: Relationship behavior without the relationship title — intimacy real, terms undefined, exit costless. Tried on the Mythbuster: real and rising, short of “the dominant form.”

entries.title: Post-wall
entries.synopsis: Manosphere shorthand for a woman past 30, spoken of as expired. The site’s read of the actual curves: a slope everyone walks at different grades, not a cliff one sex falls off.

entries.title: Pick-me
entries.synopsis: The label thrown at a woman who says out loud how women tend to behave. Rarely a rebuttal — usually social policing that reframes honesty as betrayal.

entries.title: Abundance blindness
entries.synopsis: The flood of low-effort attention women receive hides how scarce attention is for average men — each side generalizes its own inbox and misreads the other’s market.

entries.title: The Abundance Trap
entries.synopsis: What visible abundance does to the chooser: with the whole distribution on screen, evaluation replaces connection and standards drift without the market moving. Choice overload survives replication only as a conditional effect — and dating sits where the conditions concentrate. Lab find · 2026-07-26 · Pew 2023

entries.title: 4B
entries.synopsis: The Korean women’s refusal movement — no dating, sex, marriage, childbirth. Cited as the women’s strike, but the timing undercuts the causal story: Korea went sub-replacement in 1983, decades before the hashtag.

entries.title: Halo effect
entries.synopsis: The “beautiful is good” bias: one strong trait — usually looks — colors how every other trait gets read. Real and replicated, and a big slice of why the looks lever leaks into all the others.

entries.title: Friend zone
entries.synopsis: Where one-sided desire gets parked and the friendship is the consolation prize. Real as an asymmetry; toxic when treated as a debt owed — see the emotional harem for the exploitative version.

entries.title: The Black Pill
entries.synopsis: Constraint awareness pushed to fatalism: looks and fixed traits matter more than polite society admits (true), so it’s hopeless (false).

entries.title: The Height Pill
entries.synopsis: Height as destiny. The premium is real and fixed — but “it’s over under six feet” is fatalism. The curve is a window, not a ladder.

entries.title: Looksmaxxing
entries.synopsis: Maximizing physical attractiveness. Soft-maxxing (grooming, fitness, style) genuinely works; surgery-chasing and PSL despair is mostly cope.

entries.title: Mogging
entries.synopsis: To visibly outrank someone on looks, height, or status in a shared space. A real perception effect, inflated into constant ranking anxiety.

entries.title: LMS (Looks · Money · Status)
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s claim that attraction reduces to three things you can’t change. They matter — but it drops charm and exposure, the two you can move.

entries.title: PSL
entries.synopsis: The looksmaxxing forums’ 0–10 facial scale, graded to the decimal and treated as destiny. The site’s Face Calc scores in it — and rejects the fatalism it ships with.

entries.title: Chad & Stacy
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s top-tier archetypes — the man and woman the market’s rules supposedly never touch. Useful shorthand for the top band; corrosive as a story that everyone below it lost.

entries.title: Incel / femcel
entries.synopsis: Involuntarily celibate. A real predicament at the market’s bottom band — and an identity that hardens the predicament into a life sentence the data doesn’t sign.

entries.title: Normie
entries.synopsis: The ladder’s broad middle — unremarkable by PSL lights, which is most people. The insult quietly concedes the blackpill’s problem: the average face still pairs.

entries.title: The Bone Pill
entries.synopsis: The claim that attraction is mostly face, face is mostly bone, and your skeleton is a verdict. The features are real and people agree at first glance — then the agreement dissolves on acquaintance.

entries.title: The Face Pill
entries.synopsis: The Bone Pill’s retail version: your face reduced to one scoreable verdict. Three of the four facial layers are improvable; the pill launders a real input into a sealed sentence.

entries.title: Canthal tilt
entries.synopsis: The angle from inner to outer eye corner — PSL’s favorite millimeter. Its link to attractiveness is essentially unstudied: a load-bearing metric with no load-bearing evidence.

entries.title: “It’s over”
entries.synopsis: The blackpill’s verdict-phrase: fixed traits already decided your romantic life. The data behind it shows penalties and slopes — windows, not verdicts.

entries.title: The Red Pill
entries.synopsis: Dating as a market of incentives and leverage. Its gift is agency — build your value, read signals. Its poison is contempt dressed up as realism.

entries.title: Hypergamy
entries.synopsis: The drive to “marry up” in status. Real as a tilt (women weight status more), false as an iron law (educational hypergamy has reversed).

entries.title: Body count
entries.synopsis: A partner’s number of prior lovers, claimed to wreck pair-bonding. Real as a confounded correlation with divorce; false as the “oxytocin runs out” mechanism.

entries.title: AF/BB (Alpha Fucks, Beta Bucks)
entries.synopsis: The dual-mating claim that women take genes from hot men and provision from stable ones. The ovulatory-shift mechanism behind it fails to replicate.

entries.title: AWALT (All Women Are Like That)
entries.synopsis: The doctrine that women share one hidden nature. Where strategy curdles into contempt — a blanket claim that can’t survive contact with actual people.

entries.title: Frame
entries.synopsis: Holding your own center instead of begging the room to validate you. At its best, calm self-command; at its worst, performative dominance.

entries.title: Preselection
entries.synopsis: Being visibly wanted makes you more wanted. Real social proof — but it shifts how value is read, it doesn’t create attraction from nothing.

entries.title: Statusmaxxing
entries.synopsis: Building status and resources as a man’s main lever. Sound — a man’s value is status-elastic — but prestige beats borrowed dominance theater.

entries.title: The Charm Ceiling
entries.synopsis: How far “game” can carry you past looks. Access-gated, not value-gated: near-zero online, full-strength in a social circle.

entries.title: Game
entries.synopsis: Learned social and seduction skill — the red pill’s answer to fixed looks. Real but access-gated: near-zero power online, full strength inside a social circle.

entries.title: The 80/20 rule
entries.synopsis: The claim that female desire funnels to the top fifth of men. Real as app-attention skew; false as a pairing lock-out — tried on the Mythbuster, and the lock-out doesn’t hold.

entries.title: High-value man
entries.synopsis: A man high on the SMV stack — looks, money, status, charm, exposure compounding. A market read; the trouble starts when “high-value” gets read as “high-worth.”

entries.title: The Inversion
entries.synopsis: Past some SMV threshold the market flips: he stops offering and starts filtering, and women compete for access. Asserted constantly, measured never — the site files it as a Lens, not a fact.

entries.title: The Men’s Strike
entries.synopsis: The fantasy that coordinated male withdrawal would reset the market. The coordinated strike can’t hold (defection pays); the uncoordinated one is already here — and isn’t producing the reset.

entries.title: MGTOW
entries.synopsis: Men Going Their Own Way — exit as ideology. The site’s read: a label for a withdrawal already underway, not its engine.

entries.title: The Status Trade
entries.synopsis: The model naming the real kernel in hypergamy: beauty traded against status. Tested against the data, the trade is eroding as women’s earnings rise — fading, not hardening.

entries.title: Simp
entries.synopsis: A man over-investing attention and resources in someone who prices him at zero. The insult overshoots — but the underlying exchange rate is worth auditing.

entries.title: Emotional harem
entries.synopsis: The bench of “just friends” men kept for validation and support while romantic interest goes elsewhere. Being on the bench doesn’t make you special — it makes you useful.

entries.title: Monk mode
entries.synopsis: Withdrawing from the market to grind self-improvement — money, body, skills. Sound as a season; cope when it becomes a permanent excuse never to re-enter.

entries.title: The Blue Pill
entries.synopsis: Romance as sincere, fair, and personality-driven. Keeps the human center — warmth, trust — but denies the thresholds that decide who gets considered.

entries.title: Just be yourself
entries.synopsis: Healthy as authenticity; harmful when it means refusing to improve presentation, social skill, or exposure.

entries.title: There’s someone for everyone
entries.synopsis: Comforting, but not what the base rates show — especially for below-average men. Patience is wise; passivity isn’t.

entries.title: Personality matters
entries.synopsis: True but incomplete. Personality deepens and sustains attraction — usually after a first physical filter is passed.

entries.title: The One / the right person
entries.synopsis: Useful as patience, dangerous as passivity. The right person still has to meet you, notice you, want you, and choose you.

entries.title: “No good men left”
entries.synopsis: The female-side scarcity story. The men exist; the honest versions of the complaint are about the overlap — attraction, standards, and timing — not the census.

entries.title: The spark
entries.synopsis: Butterflies read as destiny. Often the opposite: the flutter spikes on uncertainty and intensity — the exact things that make a bond unstable. Excitement and fit are not the same person.

entries.title: Relationships Throughout History
entries.synopsis: “Marriage as we know it is the anomaly, not the baseline.”

entries.title: Third Spaces
entries.synopsis: “The apps didn’t win the courtship market. The places where people met were demolished first.”

entries.title: Relationships by Country
entries.synopsis: “The West didn’t invent the unbundling. It was just the pilot program.”

entries.title: What the Wall Actually Is
entries.synopsis: “Not a cliff at 30 — a slope that everyone walks, at different grades.”

entries.title: Single Parenthood
entries.synopsis: “Death built it, divorce rebuilt it, choice runs it now — and America leads the world by three to one.”

entries.title: Relationships Throughout History
entries.synopsis: Marriage as we know it is the anomaly, not the baseline. A Deep Dive tracing how alliance, religion, industry, and the modern love-match each rewrote what a relationship was for — from 3500 BC to now.
boundaryConditions: Historical institutions and incentives explain context; they do not supply one timeless natural law for intimate behavior.
pressureTests: Does the proposed rule survive societies with different property, kinship, fertility, labor, and courtship institutions?

entries.title: The Alliance Era
entries.synopsis: For most of recorded history, a wedding joined two families rather than two people. The couple stood at the center of a contract they had not written and could not easily break, closer to the terms of the deal than to the parties making it. Their assignment was to be joined, exchanged, and made to produce: an heir, an alliance, a claim on land.

entries.title: The Church Rewrites the Rules
entries.synopsis: When the Roman order gave way to the medieval Church, the institution inherited the alliance system intact and then, across centuries, quietly edited it. The Church’s strangest innovation was a single requirement: consent. It spent generations insisting that what actually made a marriage was the freely given “I do” of the two people, not the father’s signature and not the transfer of property.

entries.title: The Early Modern Turn
entries.synopsis: If the Middle Ages carry an undeserved reputation for child brides, the early modern centuries carry one for prudishness, the buttoned-up world of stern sermons and unbroken chastity before the wedding. That reputation is just as false. In the rural English parishes of the late sixteenth century a startling share of brides walked to the altar visibly pregnant. The demographer P.E.H.

entries.title: The Love-Match Revolution
entries.synopsis: Then the ground moved, and it moved because of work. Industrialization pulled production out of the household and into the factory and the office, dismantling the economic logic that had underwritten marriage for five thousand years.

entries.title: The Great Unbundling
entries.synopsis: The conclusion is worth stating bluntly, because so much modern argument is built on getting it backwards. The version of marriage nostalgia treats as timeless (the young couple, the single male breadwinner, the house full of children, the wife at home) was not history’s baseline but a brief, freakish dip.

entries.title: Third Spaces
entries.synopsis: The apps didn't win the courtship market — the third places where people used to meet were emptied out first. A Deep Dive tracing where courtship actually happened, from the well and the agora to the age of the app.
boundaryConditions: Third spaces can increase repeated, legible interaction but do not guarantee chemistry or make communities mere dating funnels.
pressureTests: Does the claimed effect persist when exposure is plentiful but reciprocity, trust, or demographic fit is absent?

entries.title: The Well and the Agora
entries.synopsis: Every settlement that has ever existed needed a place to draw water, and so every settlement had a place where, sooner or later, everyone turned up. The well, the spring, the public fountain: the young came to them alongside the old, because water admitted no exceptions, and in the coming and going a good deal of looking got done. Nobody built a well to make marriages.

entries.title: Parish and Fair
entries.synopsis: When the classical city receded, its gathering places did not vanish so much as change management. For the thousand years between the fall of Rome and the Reformation, the two dependable venues of ordinary European life were the parish church and the seasonal fair, and between them they set the rhythm of courtship for most of the population that ever lived.

entries.title: The Coffeehouse Century
entries.synopsis: Then something genuinely new appeared: a gathering place you paid a small coin to enter, built for no purpose but company itself. The coffeehouse reached England in the 1650s and multiplied fast, and around it grew a whole ecology of commercial sociability — the tavern and the public house, the assembly room, the pleasure garden, the salon.

entries.title: The Golden Age of Joining
entries.synopsis: By the last decades of the nineteenth century the gathering place had multiplied into something like a dense mesh laid over ordinary life. This was the golden age of joining: lodges and mutual-aid societies, unions and congregations, choirs and clubs and bowling leagues and fraternal orders, and above all the new commercial palaces of leisure — the dance hall, the department store, the amusement park.

entries.title: The Great Emptying
entries.synopsis: The turn comes around 1960, and it is worth stating flatly: the third space drained. Suburbanization spread people thin across the map; the car privatized the journey that used to throw strangers together; the television, and then the screen in every pocket, privatized the evening. Membership in the joined institutions fell, decade over decade, in nearly every category at once.

entries.title: Relationships by Country
entries.synopsis: The unbundling of marriage and childbearing is a wave crossing the whole world at different speeds, not a uniquely Western event. A Deep Dive comparing where the relationship transition has reached region by region — from ultra-low-fertility East Asia through Latin America, South Asia, and the Middle East to high-fertility sub-Saharan Africa.
boundaryConditions: Country comparisons are ecological context, not a license to assign every resident the national average.
pressureTests: Does the conclusion survive within-country variation by age, class, region, urbanization, and cohort?

entries.title: East Asia
entries.synopsis: Begin where the wave has traveled furthest. More than half the countries on Earth, holding a clear majority of the world’s people, now have fertility below the level that replaces a generation, and the line keeps moving outward. East Asia is where it has moved farthest and fastest.

entries.title: Latin America
entries.synopsis: Latin America runs the experiment in almost the opposite order and arrives at the same place. Marriage here never held the monopoly it holds in East Asia. Across much of the continent, couples have for generations formed households, raised children, and stayed together without ever registering a wedding — the unión libre, the free union, a socially accepted arrangement with roots that run back centuries.

entries.title: South Asia
entries.synopsis: India poses a harder question: what happens to the birth rate when the old marriage system does not loosen at all? Marriage in India remains close to universal and, for most people, arranged. Families still vet and select partners, weigh caste and community and dowry, and broker the match; the couple’s own preference has grown but still sits inside a decision the two families largely make together.

entries.title: Middle East & North Africa
entries.synopsis: No country has fallen faster than Iran, and none makes the point more sharply, because Iran spent decades trying, with the full weight of the state, to steer its birth rate: first up, then down, then up again — and lost the wheel every time.

entries.title: Sub-Saharan Africa
entries.synopsis: End where the wave has barely arrived. Sub-Saharan Africa holds the highest fertility on Earth and the youngest populations, and it is the one large region where marriage, children, and kinship still look roughly as they did across most of human history: early and near-universal marriage, bride-wealth passing between families, and, in a wide belt across the middle of the continent, polygyny that is still openly and…

entries.title: What the Wall Actually Is
entries.synopsis: The wall isn't a cliff at 30 — it's three different curves the discourse fuses into one birthday: desirability, fertility, and marriage-market position. A Deep Dive that walks each one separately, band by band, and lets it peak where the evidence puts it. Extends the Wall card from the Frameworks page.
boundaryConditions: The essay separates attention, fertility, age preferences, and actual pairing rather than treating them as one outcome.
pressureTests: Which component moves first, which merely correlates with age, and which remains viable despite the average slope?

entries.title: 18 to 25
entries.synopsis: The wall is the most repeated claim there is about women and age, and it arrives as a single event on a single birthday. Youth is the asset, youth peaks in the early twenties, and somewhere around thirty the whole thing drops off a cliff, after which a woman is spoken of as post-wall. The picture is vivid and portable, which is most of why it travels as far as it does. It is also fused.

entries.title: 26 to 31
entries.synopsis: By these years the app-desirability line has already tipped downward for women, and in the wall’s telling the window is closing fast. Set beside the actual timing of marriage, the alarm looks misplaced. The median American woman marries for the first time near the top of this band, not before it — and the median man a couple of years later still.

entries.title: 32 to 37
entries.synopsis: Here is the part of the wall that is not a myth, and it deserves a fair hearing before anything is subtracted from it. Fertility genuinely declines with age, and it does so on a schedule the other curves do not share. This is the one gradient that comes from the body rather than the market, and its real turn falls inside these years.

entries.title: 38 to 49
entries.synopsis: Past the fertility inflection comes the curve the culture watches hardest of all — the age gap between partners. It has been measured directly, and the measurement is unambiguous about its direction.

entries.title: 50 and Up
entries.synopsis: The wall’s mirror claim is that men age like wine, their value climbing while a woman’s falls. The same Bruch and Newman curve that anchors the female slope carries the male one, and it does rise — for a while. Men’s app-desirability climbs through the thirties and forties and peaks around 50, and then it too turns down. “Ages like wine” describes the first half of a curve and quietly drops the second.

entries.title: Single Parenthood
entries.synopsis: The one-parent home is not new — it changed owners. Death built it, divorce rebuilt it, and the never-married route runs it now, with America leading the world at 23% of children in solo-parent households against a 7% global share. A Deep Dive that walks the century, the custody split, the class gradient, and what the outcome data actually survives scrutiny. Extends the single-parenthood charts on the Statistics page.

entries.title: 1900 to 1959: The Widow’s House
entries.synopsis: No figure in the gender discourse works harder than the single mother. One side reads her as the proof of male abandonment, the other as the price of female choices, and the statistics posters have her raising 85% of the youth in prison and most of the dropouts and runaways besides — numbers that close arguments precisely because nobody checks them. This essay checks them.

entries.title: 1960 to 1979: Divorce Rebuilds It
entries.synopsis: When the Census Bureau first drew its modern series in 1968, the old world was still largely intact: 85% of American children lived with two parents, 11% with their mother only, 1% with their father only. Then the legal ground moved.

entries.title: 1980 to 1999: The Route In Flips
entries.synopsis: The divorce boom crested around 1980 and receded. The single-parent share kept climbing anyway, because the route into the one-parent home was changing underneath it: children stopped arriving in marriages that later broke, and started arriving outside marriage in the first place.

entries.title: 2000 to 2019: The World’s Highest
entries.synopsis: Where did the curve land? Higher than anywhere else on Earth. Not among the highest — the highest, of every country measured.

entries.title: The 2020s: The Ledger
entries.synopsis: So what does the one-adult house actually cost? The honest answer has three entries: a money line that is brutal and undisputed, an outcomes line that is real but smaller than advertised, and a meme line that is mostly fabricated. They deserve to be kept apart.

entries.title: SMV Calculator
entries.synopsis: A structured assessment of Looks, Money, Status, Charm, and Exposure. This is not a moral score. It is a market-position read: what creates attention, leverage, and realistic options.
boundaryConditions: The output is a structured self-assessment under LE's stated model, not an objective rank, diagnosis, or promise of response.
commonMisreadings: A calculator estimate should not be treated as more precise or universal than its self-reported inputs.
pressureTests: How does the result change when market, context, evidence quality, or evaluator assumptions change?

entries.title: Compatibility Calculator
entries.synopsis: Score any of the four Love Hierarchies, factor by factor. The headline shows the full weighted score and its band — nothing is capped. The framework line beneath it names any structural breach the profile trips — a sub-5 metric, a failed 7–7 Rule, an uncleared gate — so a high number can’t quietly hide a tanked core factor.
boundaryConditions: The tool can organize known information and flag mismatches; it cannot establish live chemistry or future durability.
pressureTests: Which high-scoring pair fails in person, and which unmeasured factor explains the miss?

entries.title: Face Calculator
entries.synopsis: Drop in a face — on your device, nothing uploaded — and it reads everything it can from the photo, then scores it two ways: the Black Pill (PSL) lens and a conventional one. No sliders. It pairs with the Body Calc, and the two combine into an Overall looks rating below.
boundaryConditions: Image-derived proportions are sensitive to pose, lens, lighting, landmark placement, and the model's limited construct.
commonMisreadings: Facial measurements are not a full judgment of attractiveness, health, identity, or worth.

entries.title: Body Calculator
entries.synopsis: Drop in a full-body photo — on your device, nothing uploaded — and it reads the frame it can from the silhouette, then scores it two ways: the Black Pill lens and a conventional one. No sliders. It pairs with the Face Calc, and the two combine into an Overall looks rating below.
boundaryConditions: Body estimates depend on self-report and simplified proportions; they are not medical or diagnostic outputs.
commonMisreadings: A model category is not a universal attractiveness verdict or health assessment.

entries.title: Matchmaker
entries.synopsis: Not a flattering list — the realistic intersection. It takes your own value profile (pulled from your SMV, Face and Body calcs), asks what you want, then finds the celebrities you'd actually match with at your level — and gives each one a full Love Hierarchy breakdown: every factor scored, every factor explained. Flip By Looks / By SMV to change which scale it pairs you on.
boundaryConditions: The instrument compares declared profiles and constraints; every suggested match remains subject to reciprocity and live interaction.
commonMisreadings: Algorithmic compatibility does not create consent, attraction, or an obligation to meet.
pressureTests: Which suggested match fails after reciprocal choice and the Interaction Gate are applied?
